review: Volume doesn't guarantee quality, but the Model Y mostly backs up its sales chart position. From €44,990, the entry Standard RWD claims 500km WLTP from a 62.5kWh pack and does 0-100km/h in 5.9 seconds — brisk rather than violent. The real advantage is Tesla's Supercharger network: a 175kW peak gets you 10-80% in roughly 27 minutes, with reliability across Europe that rivals still can't match. Ride quality divides opinion — without air suspension, the base car gets properly bumpy around town, and motorway road noise creeps in through single-pane glass. Real-world efficiency also falls short of Tesla's claims, with testers logging closer to 3.3 rather than the promised 4.5 miles per kWh. Where it wins outright is practicality: an 854-litre boot plus frunk embarrasses every mid-size SUV rival, and cabin space is genuinely generous. No CarPlay, touchscreen-only controls, and a firm ride are the price of admission.

The Elroq is proof Skoda understands what mainstream buyers actually want. From €33,900 for the 50 with a 52kWh battery and 375km WLTP range, it undercuts nearly everything in its class while still delivering a genuinely composed motorway ride and supportive seats. Push it over broken tarmac or big potholes, though, and the suspension wallows more than you'd like. It isn't a driver's car — steering is light and remote — but nobody's cross-shopping an Elroq for cornering. Charging tops out around 145kW on the base pack (175kW on the 85), enough for a 25-minute 10-80% stop without becoming a chore. The 470-litre boot trails segment leaders like the Enyaq, but clever storage — an umbrella holder, ice scraper, cable nets — softens the blow. For value alone, this is currently one of the smartest electric SUVs money can buy in Europe.

Renault's reborn 5 is the rare EV that photographs as well as it drives — and unusually for a city car, it actually drives well. From €24,990 with the 40kWh Urban Range battery (308km WLTP), or stretch to the 52kWh Comfort Range for roughly 405km, and it's genuinely fun in traffic with grown-up manners on A-roads. The infotainment is unusually intuitive for the segment. The compromises are real, though: rear legroom is tight for adults over six feet, the 326-litre boot has an awkward lip, and DC charging peaks at just 80-100kW, meaning 15-80% takes around 30 minutes — slow by 2025 standards. Real-world range testing has come in a little under WLTP figures too. None of that dents the core appeal — this is an EV built around charm and everyday usability rather than outright numbers, and pricing this aggressive makes it one of Europe's best-value electric cars.

The Model 3 remains the most complete Tesla for the money. From €36,990, the Standard RWD pairs a 62.5kWh battery with 513km WLTP range and a genuinely quick 6.1-second 0-100km/h — figures that still embarrass most combustion saloons at this price. The Supercharger network again does the heavy lifting on longer trips, with a 170-250kW peak getting a 10-80% top-up done in around 27 minutes. Reviewers praise the flat rear floor and generous legroom, though cost-cutting on the base trim shows in cloth seat inserts and the loss of ventilation. The 594-litre boot plus 88-litre frunk beats most rivals, even if the narrow saloon opening is less versatile than a hatchback's. Ride comfort is decent rather than plush — there's no adaptive damping on entry trims — and the minimalist, screen-only cabin remains a love-it-or-leave-it proposition. As outright value for range and pace, few EVs at this price compete.

The ID.3 was meant to be VW's Model 3 killer, and while it never quite landed that blow, it's matured into a solid, if unexciting, hatchback. From €35,990 for the Pro with a 59kWh battery, WLTP range lands around 421km. Charging peaks at 145kW, enough for a 28-minute 10-80% session. On motorways it's genuinely refined and comfortable; around town, particularly on larger wheels, the ride turns jiggly over rough surfaces. Base powertrains feel sluggish, and even the punchier GTX doesn't translate that power into fun on a twisty road. The 385-litre boot is adequately shaped rather than class-leading, and rear space is tight for three adults. Against cheaper rivals like the MG4, the ID.3 can feel pricey for what it delivers — competent, but rarely exciting.

If there's a default answer to 'which electric family SUV should I buy,' it's increasingly the Enyaq. From €39,900 for the 60 with a 59kWh battery and roughly 429km WLTP range, it combines a genuinely spacious cabin with a 585-litre boot (1,710 litres folded) that shames most mid-size rivals. Motorway refinement is a highlight — the ride smooths out further as speed rises — though low-speed surfaces can feel jiggly on bigger wheels. Performance is adequate rather than exciting; this is a car built for relaxed A-to-B driving, not back roads. Charging peaks around 150kW, delivering a 10-80% top-up in about 25 minutes. Real-world efficiency of roughly 3.8-4.1mi/kWh holds up well against Skoda's claims. This is sensible, well-equipped, genuinely accommodating family transport that undercuts pricier VW Group siblings without an obvious downside.

The ID.4 shares its bones with the Enyaq and ID.3, but somehow ends up feeling the least convincing of the three. From €38,995 with a 52kWh entry battery giving 357km WLTP, it's roomy in the back with genuine headroom for tall passengers and comfortable, supportive front seats for long stints. But the interior feels cheap for the money, the touchscreen-heavy infotainment is fiddly to operate on the move, and the 543-litre boot has an awkwardly high loading lip. Charging tops out at 135-185kW depending on battery, translating to roughly 28 minutes for a 10-80% top-up — competitive, if unremarkable. Base powertrains lack punch, and cheaper VW Group stablemates — the Skoda Elroq especially — offer better interior quality and styling for less money. It's a reasonable, quiet-riding SUV, but in a class this competitive, 'reasonable' isn't enough to stand out.

VW's electric answer to the Passat is the ID.7, and it plays the long-distance cruiser role convincingly. From €56,995, the Pro's 77kWh battery delivers a substantial 615km WLTP range, with a genuine 300 real-world miles achievable — long-legged for a mainstream EV. The 175kW peak charging gets a 10-80% top-up done in around 28 minutes. Ride comfort at speed is a highlight: wind noise is minimal and the cabin stays composed even at motorway pace, while the 532-litre boot (1,586 litres folded) and generous rear legroom make it a genuinely practical family saloon. What it lacks is any sense of occasion — the button-free, monochrome dashboard feels austere, and it's simply not fun on a twisty road. Positioned against price-comparable rivals it offers strong range-per-euro, even if VW's three-year warranty undercuts Kia's far more generous seven-year cover.

BMW's smallest EV promises premium polish but doesn't fully deliver it. From €42,900, the eDrive20's 64.7kWh battery returns around 475km WLTP, with 0-100km/h in 8.6 seconds — adequate rather than quick. The bigger issue is the ride: over broken urban tarmac and speed bumps, the stiff suspension makes itself felt constantly, even though things settle down nicely at motorway speeds. Charging peaks at just 130kW, meaning a 10-80% stop takes around 29 minutes — noticeably behind rivals like the Tesla Model Y or Volvo EX30. Cabin materials are genuinely nice and the infotainment is slick and responsive, but the 490-litre boot is unremarkable for the class, and pricing puts it uncomfortably close to larger, more practical alternatives like the Skoda Elroq. It's a competent, well-built small SUV, but BMW's usual dynamic sparkle is largely absent.

The EV3 is Kia's answer to the compact-SUV EV brief, and it's a genuinely strong one. From €35,990, the Standard Range's 58.3kWh battery delivers 436km WLTP, with the 81.4kWh Long Range stretching to a genuinely useful 605km. The boxy shape pays real dividends inside: rear legroom beats rivals like the Volvo EX30, and the 460-litre boot ranks among the best in its class. The ride is quiet, refined and comfortable, if a little lumbering over successive rough patches thanks to its weight. Charging peaks at 102-127kW depending on battery — decent, not outstanding. A 10-80% top-up takes around 29-31 minutes. On the road it's smooth and easy rather than sporty, with steering that feels remote on B-roads. Interior plastics on base trims feel a little cheap, but comprehensive standard equipment and Kia's excellent seven-year warranty make this one of Europe's smartest-value electric SUVs.

The Q4 e-tron is comfortable and desirable in the way Audis are supposed to be, but the value equation doesn't quite add up. From €45,900, the 63kWh entry battery returns 411km WLTP, with 0-100km/h taking a leisurely 8.5 seconds. The ride is genuinely comfortable and composed over poor surfaces, though spongy brakes undermine confidence when stopping hard. Real-world efficiency testing has shown a noticeable gap versus Audi's claims — closer to 3.4mi/kWh against a claimed 4.0. Charging peaks around 135-175kW depending on spec, with a 10-80% stop taking roughly 28 minutes. The 520-litre boot trails class leaders, and interior quality post-facelift has taken a step back, with scratchy plastics appearing on lower door cards. Set against cheaper, roomier VW Group siblings like the Enyaq or ID.4, the Q4's premium badge is doing a lot of the pricing work here.

Audi's newest electric SUV is genuinely fast to charge and genuinely comfortable at speed — it's just hard to call it exciting. From €58,900, the entry quattro's 94.9kWh battery claims up to 580km WLTP, and 270kW peak DC charging delivers a 10-80% top-up in a class-leading 22 minutes. Air suspension irons out big obstacles beautifully on faster roads but turns jittery over smaller urban imperfections, and at 2.3 tonnes, the Q6 makes its weight known under braking and through corners. Real-world efficiency has disappointed in testing — closer to 3.0mi/kWh against a claimed 3.9, roughly 79% of the advertised range. Practically, it's a genuinely big, bulky thing to park, though a 526-litre boot plus 64-litre front trunk for charging cables adds usefulness. Against similarly priced rivals like the BMW iX3 or a well-specced Model Y, the Q6 feels pleasant rather than genuinely compelling.

The Born is the ID.3's spicier sibling, and mostly succeeds at making the underlying platform more desirable. From €38,750, the 59kWh battery delivers around 423km WLTP, with claimed efficiency of 3.9-4.3mi/kWh that largely holds up in real-world driving. The cabin is genuinely practical, with excellent rear legroom and supportive seats that make it a comfortable motorway cruiser. Charging peaks at up to 185kW on larger-battery versions, with a 10-80% stop taking around 24-26 minutes — competitive for the class. Where it disappoints is dynamics: despite Cupra's performance positioning, it's not all that fun to drive, with spongy brakes and no one-pedal driving mode. The infotainment system is also prone to glitches and crashes. The 385-litre boot is on the smaller side for the segment. It's a stylish, efficient, well-built EV that trades on distinctive design more than the sporting credentials its badge implies.

The EX30 is Volvo's proof that small doesn't mean slow: the Twin Motor Performance hits 100 km/h in 3.6 seconds, quicker than most hot hatches, while even the entry Single Motor manages a brisk 5.3s. That pace, paired with a genuinely plush ride over potholes and a minimalist Scandi cabin, makes it a compelling city car. The catch is the badge doesn't cover for the physics: WLTP claims evaporate fast in the real world, with testers seeing as little as 68-89% of the official figure, and the 318-litre boot is stingy for the class. Charging is a genuine strength — 26-28 minutes for 10-80% at up to 153kW is competitive. At £33,060 to start, it's not cheap for what's essentially a supermini on stilts, but nothing else in this segment feels this fast or this designed. Buy it for the drive, not the spreadsheet.

BMW's electric Gran Coupe is the rare EV that drives like a BMW first and an EV second — sharp steering, a genuinely settled motorway ride, and 282hp enough for 6.0 seconds to 100km/h without feeling like the point. The eDrive35's 70.3kWh battery returns a WLTP-rated 319 miles, broadly confirmed by independent testing, though it's the shortest-legged i4 in the range. 180kW peak charging gets 10-80% done in around 30-35 minutes, solidly mid-pack. Where it stumbles is money: at £51,730 to start, tipping over the luxury-tax threshold, with resale values shedding over 60% in three years, the i4 asks a lot for what is, underneath the badge, a tight-rear-legroom saloon shape. The 470-litre boot and 1,290-litre fold-flat capacity are genuinely useful, though. A brilliant thing to drive; a tough thing to justify.

Citroën's pitch here is refreshingly honest: this is a budget EV built to feel like anything but. The Advanced Comfort suspension genuinely delivers ride quality that shames larger cars, and that's the ë-C3's whole reason for being. At under £20,000 before discounts, it undercuts nearly every rival EV on sale, and the 44kWh battery's 199-mile WLTP figure is honest enough in town, even if it collapses to around 150 miles on the motorway. The 100kW peak charge rate sounds fine on paper but tails off after a few minutes, adding real time to a 20-80% top-up. Performance is unhurried rather than exciting — 0-100km/h arrives in around 11 seconds — and the boot's odd shape when folded is a minor annoyance. None of that matters much against the price. This is the small EV that finally makes electric motoring feel unremarkable, which, for once, is a compliment.

The EQA is what happens when a compact combustion SUV gets an unconvincing electric conversion. The three-pointed star and plush-adjacent cabin still charm, and the 70.5kWh battery's WLTP range of up to 345 miles is honestly delivered — the trip computer is reassuringly accurate. But everything else here has been overtaken. 100kW peak DC charging trails rivals like the BMW iX1 (130kW) and Volvo XC40 (200kW), stretching a 10-80% charge to 35 minutes. The 340-litre boot is 95 litres down on the closely related GLA, and the driving experience — light, uncommunicative steering, a firm ride over broken tarmac — never feels worth the £49,760-plus asking price. Even the base model's 8.9-second 0-100km/h feels leisurely for the money. Cheaper, roomier, faster-charging rivals from Skoda and Kia make the EQA a badge purchase, not a rational one.

The Spring exists to answer one question: how cheap can an EV get before it stops being usable? At around £14,995, it's comfortably the least expensive electric car sold in Europe, and that changes the calculus entirely. The 24.3kWh battery's 140-mile WLTP range shrinks to a genuine 110-120 miles, 0-100km/h takes a leisurely 13.7 seconds, and the 30kW peak charge rate means a 10-80% top-up eats 45 minutes. Body roll is pronounced, tyres are basic, and motorway trips feel like a chore. And yet the 308-litre boot is a genuine surprise for something this small, and as a second car for short urban commutes, nothing else gets you into electric motoring this cheaply. Judge it as a city runabout, not a family car, and the Spring makes total sense.

The 500e trades on charm, and mostly it works — that retro silhouette and cheerful cabin make it one of the few EVs that's genuinely fun to be seen in. But scratch beneath the styling and the compromises show. The larger 42kWh battery's 199-mile WLTP range is modest by 2026 standards, real-world figures land closer to 150 miles, and there's no heat pump to soften the winter hit. The 185-litre boot is minuscule, and rear seats are strictly for children or short journeys. On the plus side, 85kW peak charging gets a 10-80% top-up done in as little as 24 minutes, and 0-100km/h in 9.0 seconds feels lively around town. Pricing from roughly £24,995 puts it above rivals with more range and space. Buy the 500e for the way it makes short trips feel special — not for what it can't do beyond the city limits.

The Kona Electric remains one of the most sensible EVs you can buy, and that's meant as a genuine compliment. The 65.4kWh Long Range battery delivers a WLTP-rated 319 miles that holds up well against real-world driving, the 466-litre boot beats most rivals in the class outright, and 102kW peak charging gets a 10-80% top-up done in around 41 minutes — unspectacular but dependable. It's relaxed rather than sporty: 0-100km/h in around 8 seconds is respectable, but the light steering and soft low-speed ride give way to less composure at motorway pace, where the Skoda Elroq feels more settled. Interior quality is mixed — solid where your hands land, cheaper plastics elsewhere. At around £36,945 for the long-range trim, though, it's generously equipped and genuinely practical. This is the EV equivalent of a good pair of work boots: unglamorous, but it does the job every single day.

MG's electric hatchback remains the value benchmark this list keeps measuring against. From around £26,995, the standard 64kWh battery delivers a WLTP-rated 280 miles, and range tops out at 338 miles on the Extended Range model — genuinely competitive numbers at a price that undercuts a Volkswagen ID.3 by thousands. It's also unexpectedly good to drive: light, direct steering and rear-wheel-drive balance make it properly fun on a back road, and the range-topping XPower's 3.8-second 0-100km/h sprint embarrasses cars costing twice as much. The ride turns bouncy over undulating roads, and the 363-litre boot lags rivals, but 150kW charging (10-80% in around 35-40 minutes) is solid for the money. MG's reliability record is genuinely the worst surveyed of any brand, tempered somewhat by a seven-year warranty. Buy the MG4 with your head, not blind faith in the badge, and it's very hard to beat for the price.

Built on Volkswagen's MEB platform but wrapped in a genuinely well-judged Ford cabin, the Explorer EV is the most convincing thing to come out of this collaboration. The Extended Range model's 374-mile WLTP figure is credible — testers logged around 3.7 miles/kWh, translating to roughly 280 real miles — and 185kW peak charging delivers a 10-80% top-up in a brisk 26 minutes. The Mega Console central storage bin is a genuinely clever practicality trick, though the 470-litre boot itself trails segment leaders offering 543 litres-plus. Ride quality depends heavily on wheel size: 20-inch alloys turn fidgety over broken tarmac, 19-inch cars are noticeably more settled. Steering is sharp for something this size. From £35,175, it's priced right against the Kia EV6 and undercuts the Model Y. A genuinely likeable, slightly compromised family SUV.

BYD's smallest EV for Europe undercuts almost everything else on this list, and mostly earns the right to. From around £18,650 for the entry Active trim, or £20,064 for the better-equipped Comfort with its 43.2kWh battery and 200-mile WLTP range, it's aggressively priced against the Renault 5 and Citroën ë-C3. The catch is ride quality — it's genuinely jiggly over rough British roads, less settled than the Renault, and the cabin plastics feel every bit as cheap as the price suggests. Charging at 65-85kW peak isn't quick, but a 30-minute 10-80% top-up is workable. The Comfort's 154bhp motor is the only version worth having, cutting 0-100km/h to a reasonably brisk 8 seconds; lesser trims feel genuinely slow. Strictly four seats and a usefully square 308-litre boot round out a car that's better value than it is polished — which, at this price, is a fair trade.

The T03 is proof that Chinese manufacturers can now build a genuinely credible budget EV, not just a cheap one. At £15,995, it undercuts almost every rival while still fitting a panoramic sunroof and a properly roomy cabin for four. The trade-offs are real, though: 0-100km/h takes a lazy 12.7 seconds, the 165-mile WLTP range drops to around 144 miles in mixed driving, and 48kW peak charging means a 10-80% top-up can stretch past 50 minutes at some chargers. The 210-litre boot is genuinely tiny, and the touchscreen-only control layout — no Apple CarPlay or Android Auto — grates daily. Ride quality in town is better than the price suggests, if floatier once you hit motorway speeds. Judged purely as cut-price city transport, the T03 undercuts the Dacia Spring on kit if not outright value.

The EQB is the pragmatist's Mercedes: a genuinely usable seven-seat electric SUV built on ageing GLB bones, and it shows. The 70.5kWh battery's WLTP range tops out at 324 miles on the 250+, trailing rivals like the BMW iX1 only marginally, but well behind the segment's newer entrants. Acceleration is unhurried by design — 8.9 seconds to 100km/h on the base front-drive model — because this is a car for wafting, not overtaking. Where it earns its keep is space: 495 litres with five seats up, 1,710 folded, and a third row that's tight but genuinely usable for children. Charging at up to 112kW gets a 10-80% top-up done in around 30 minutes, competitive if unspectacular. At £52,810-plus, it's expensive if you don't actually need the extra seats — and pointless if you don't.
